entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

print(n)
EOF

content.text:
The work is implemented and validated, but not committed. It lives in a separate worktree, `/home/mike/nexus-cc` on branch `feat/compaction-continuity` (from `origin/main` `a58f860`). Your installed `nexus` and `~/nexus-code` are untouched, and nothing in homelab-ai was changed, deployed or promoted.

**Why the separate worktree.** During my usage-limit pause `main` was reset to `origin/main`, earlier state was stashed, and someone left uncommitted edits in `~/nexus-code`. Those included a partial start on this task. You asked me to verify what had landed: nothing had. I didn't build on edits I couldn't attribute.

**Verdicts**
- **Standalone Nexus: accepted, on scripted and live evidence.** Everything works without homelab-ai. Missing capabilities fall back to your configuration or labelled defaults, and losing one never fails a turn. I did not run it live against a non-gateway server; that case rests on scripted tests.
- **homelab-ai integration: accepted for the current contract, with one requirement unmet on the gateway side.** Nexus can't get a token count guaranteed to match the request inference admits. `/v1/tokenize` counts on the first available worker and skips the routing and reasoning policy that inference applies first. So Nexus labels counts as "exact on the counted worker", compares them with the gateway's own post-admission count, and reports any worker difference. The handoff proposes the gateway change; Nexus works either way.

**What changed**
- **No step ceiling.** The 300-step and 120-minute defaults are gone, the 8/15-step cap on helper agents is gone, and the "finish now, steps are running out" prompts appear only under a limit you set. Limits you set still apply.
- **Repetition judged against workspace state.** An action counts as repeated only when the action, its result and the workspace content are all unchanged:
  - **Retries:** a retry after a real change is legitimate.
  - **Not progress:** plan edits, identical rewrites and output that differs only in timestamps.
  - **Polls and transient failures:** waited out with backoff, 1 to 30 seconds, instead of being treated as loops.
  - **Unknown workspace state:** reported as unknown rather than treated as unchanged.
- **Tracking that survives.** Step counts, loops, failed approaches and compactions now belong to the objective, so they survive compaction, a "continue" follow-up and `/resume`.
- **Compaction is a durable boundary.**
  - **Commit order:** the original messages are saved to the archive first, then the task state, then the session.
  - **Write failures:** shown, and an automatic compaction that can't be saved stops the turn.
  - **`/compact` during work:** queued until the current model call and its tool calls have finished, with an acknowledgement and an outcome for each request.
- **Sizing from the provider.** The context window and output allowance come from the gateway when it advertises them, otherwise from `--context-limit` or labelled defaults. Requests are counted with the exact body Nexus sends. `/status` and each turn's result say where every number came from. `--strict-token-count` is opt-in.

**Live runs found three bugs the scripted tests had missed; all are fixed with regression tests**
- **Run 1:** after compaction trimmed file contents, the model re-read them and Nexus stopped the turn as a loop. Re-reads after compaction are now recorded as context thrash, separately from repetition.
- **Run 2:** compaction mid-turn silently detached the live tracking record, so the saved step count was wrong.
- **Run 2:** each request was counted twice when your limit was below the advertised window.

**Run 3**, a 50-step task on a 32k window, completed:
- **Compaction:** 15 compactions, all recorded.
- **Counting:** every request counted exactly by the gateway; Nexus's own estimate ran 35–55% high.
- **Delivered:** 13 tests pass, and no existing function changed.
- **Model behaviour:** the model deleted padding comments it wasn't asked to touch, and the new code is covered only by tests it wrote.

**Tests**
- 65 new tests, including a real 311-step run and three tests that kill the process at points inside the compaction save.
- Final `make test` on a snapshot identical to the worktree's code: 266 Rust tests and 899/899 CLI tests pass, and all security gates pass.
- The full-suite run before that had 17 failures. All were fixed; the ledger lists each change.
- Two existing tests changed meaning: their test servers now ignore capability reads, and the abort test waits for the model call to start instead of a fixed 200 ms.

**Not done**
- Nothing is committed or merged into your installed build.
- No live run without the gateway, and no live capacity or worker change; the gateway didn't change during the session.
- No live `/compact` through the TUI; the TUI's message path is tested.
- `graphify update` was skipped: there's no graph in the worktree, and I left the main checkout alone.

**Costs**
- Workspace state checks add about 50–140 ms per step.
- Saves forced to disk add about 50 ms each, but only at compaction saves, segment checkpoints and turn ends. Saves between those survive a crash but not a power loss.

**Files** (all in `/home/mike/nexus-cc`)
- `docs/reviews/2026-10-13-compaction-continuity-acceptance.md` — the acceptance ledger
- `docs/reviews/2026-10-13-homelab-ai-gateway-capability-handoff.md` — the gateway handoff
- `docs/COMPACTION_AND_CONTINUITY.md` — operator and developer guide
- `docs/reviews/evidence/2026-10-13-compaction-continuity/` — live-run logs, build identities, tracking dumps

content.text:
Mine is the better solution for this brief. Each point was checked against the code, or by running it:

| Requirement | Uncommitted edits in `~/nexus-code` | Branch `feat/compaction-continuity` (`73489bd`) |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Request token counting | `countTokensRemote` is defined but never called | Used before every gateway request; counted live on all 50 steps of run 3 |
| Body that gets counted | `{model, messages, tools}` built separately, without the egress checks inference applies | The exact body inference sends, after the same egress and disclosure checks |
| Provider capability discovery | Off unless `NEXUS_DISCOVER_CAPABILITIES=1`; any `--context-limit` overrides advertised capacity entirely | On whenever the provider advertises it; a limit above advertised capacity is capped |
| Repeated failing commands | Never detected: `duration_ms` changes every run (ran: two identical failing runs → different outcome) | Detected: exit code decides failure, timing is ignored (ran: same outcome, `deterministic_failure`) |
| Plan edits counted as progress | Yes: progress signature includes the plan and `nextAction`, which the brief forbids | No |
| Automatic compaction durability | Unchanged: originals stay in memory until turn end; no session record in the save; no fsync | One ordered, synced save (archive → task state → session) shared with `/compact` |
| Polling | Detected by tool name containing "status"/"poll" | Detected from unchanged result on an unchanged workspace, with backoff |
| Evidence | Their 37 tests pass; no live run | 899/899 suite, 4 live gateway runs |

Theirs has one useful idea I lack: rewriting absolute workspace paths to relative ones when comparing tool arguments.

Their edits also include an unrelated feature: instruction precedence and knowledge scope (prompt rules plus a per-turn read-only option, with its own test). That isn't part of this work, so it shouldn't be thrown away by this merge.

**Recommended landing:**
1. Stash all of `~/nexus-code`'s uncommitted edits under a clear label, so nothing is lost and the instruction-precedence work can be recovered.
2. Fast-forward local `main` to `73489bd`.
3. Rebuild, so the installed `nexus` runs it.
4. No push.

Shall I go ahead?

# Gateway capability handoff: request counting equivalent to admission

**From:** nexus-code (`feat/compaction-continuity`, base `a58f860`). **To:** homelab-ai maintainers.
**Status:** read-only finding; nothing in homelab-ai was changed, deployed or promoted. Nexus works without any of
this. It is an integration improvement, not a dependency.

## Contract inspected

- homelab-ai `/home/mike/Projects/aihost` at `fb1a2cd95a53d3f084e1c98042f2212906622a9e` (`main`, clean).
- Deployed release `t5820-gateway-b72a4f5` (`inventory/production/host_vars/ai-5820-01.yml:257`); no later commit
  touches `orchestrator_runtime/` or `orchestrator_gateway/`.
- Verified live on 2026-10-13 from the development host (10.0.8.95) through Nexus's own client:
  - `GET /v1/models` for `engineering/b0` advertised:
    - `context_length` 65536 and `max_completion_tokens` 8192;
    - `limits_version` `a3c2fcbc2f2b977c`;
    - one serving worker, `b0-live-llama-worker1`.
  - `POST /v1/tokenize` returned `source: "exact"` with the worker id: 4420 prompt tokens with Nexus's tool
    definitions, 23 without them.

## What Nexus uses today

Nexus uses each part of the contract as it stands:

- **Capacity and output allowance**: from `/v1/models`. They are refreshed when the model, `limits_version`, the
  serving workers or the observed capacity change.
- **Pre-dispatch counting**: Nexus `POST`s the exact chat body it is about to send (messages, tools, `tool_choice`,
  temperature, `max_tokens`) to `/v1/tokenize`, on the same endpoint and with the same bearer as inference.
- **Post-dispatch evidence**: Nexus reads the admitted count and route from the inference response headers
  (`X-AIHost-Prompt-Tokens`, `-Prompt-Tokens-Source`, `-Route`, `-Context-Limit`, `-Limits-Version`).

## Requirement the current contract cannot satisfy

> For supported request counting, distinguish an exact count on the sampled worker from an exact count for the
> subsequently admitted inference request.

`/v1/tokenize` cannot give the second.

- **How tokenize picks a worker**: the first worker in the alias's `serving` list that is not capacity-blocked
  (`orchestrator_runtime/runtime.py:1070-1075`).
- **What it skips**: the router (`X-Task-Class`, attempt and previous-outcome escalation, canary, affinity, load),
  drain, circuit-breaker and model-RBAC checks.
- **What it counts**: the **raw** request, without `reasoning_policy.apply`.
- **What inference does instead** (`runtime.py:1441-1497`, `_plan` at `1109-1141`):
  1. It routes.
  2. It picks an eligible worker, with affinity.
  3. It rewrites `chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking` and `thinking_budget_tokens` (`reasoning.py:96-107`).
  4. Only then does it count and admit, re-planning if admission grants a different worker (`runtime.py:1539-1547`).

**Consequences:**

- A count can come from a different worker than the one that serves the request. For example, `X-Task-Class: review`
  routes `engineering/b0` to the deep pool while tokenize counts on lead.
- A count can come from a different template input (`enable_thinking`).
- Nexus therefore labels a pre-dispatch count `exact_sampled_worker`, never "exact for this request".
- Only the post-dispatch header count (`exact_admitted`) is exact for the admitted request, and it arrives after the
  fact.
- Strict counting (`--strict-token-count`) can require a worker count, but cannot require an admission-equivalent one.

### Related gaps found while reading

1. The vLLM adapter's tokenize omits `tool_choice` and `response_format` (`engines.py:162-170`); llama.cpp includes
   them (`engines.py:18`).
2. `limits_version` in `/v1/models` is an alias-level hash of per-worker versions that does not include the reasoning
   policy (`runtime.py:1050`). The `X-AIHost-Limits-Version` inference header carries the **per-worker** version. The
   two cannot be compared directly: live, the alias was `a3c2fcbc2f2b977c` and the per-worker header was
   `15ce8141d79a3260` for the same worker.
3. `POST /v1/tokenize` answers 404 `{"status":"not_found"}` both for an unknown model and when every worker of the
   alias is blocked (`runtime.py:1080`). A client cannot tell "unsupported" from "temporarily unavailable". Nexus
   treats a 404 that mentions blocking or capacity as unavailable, and other 404s as unsupported.
4. The tokenize response has no field saying which policy produced the count.

## Capability that would close it (proposal for homelab-ai to decide)

A counting mode equivalent to admission, as an optional addition. Existing clients keep working.

- `POST /v1/tokenize` with an opt-in (for example `"plan": "inference"`, or a header) that runs the same `_plan`
  inference would run: route with the request's `X-Task-Class` and other routing inputs, select the worker with the
  same eligibility checks, apply the reasoning policy, then count. It would return:
  - `worker_id` and `pool`;
  - the per-worker `limits_version`;
  - the effective `chat_template_kwargs` (or a digest of them);
  - `source`: `exact` / `estimated_conservative`;
  - a field such as `planned: true` stating the count used the inference plan.
- Optionally, a short-lived plan token returned by tokenize and accepted by `/v1/chat/completions` (or the existing
  `X-AIHost-Worker` pin, extended to tokenize) so the counted plan is the admitted plan.
- Distinct statuses for "unknown model" and "no eligible worker now" (for example 404 and 503).
- The vLLM tokenize adapter passing `tool_choice` and `response_format`, like llama.cpp.

**What Nexus would do with it:** label such counts `exact` (admission-equivalent) and allow strict counting to require
them. The change would sit in `cli/src/core/provider_capabilities.ts` (`parseTokenizeResponse`) and
`cli/src/client.ts` (`countRequestTokens`). Without it, Nexus keeps the current labels and the post-dispatch
comparison. Standalone operation is unaffected either way.

9	- homelab-ai `/home/mike/Projects/aihost` at `fb1a2cd95a53d3f084e1c98042f2212906622a9e` (`main`, clean).
10	- Deployed release `t5820-gateway-b72a4f5` (`inventory/production/host_vars/ai-5820-01.yml:257`); no later commit
11	  touches `orchestrator_runtime/` or `orchestrator_gateway/`.
12	- Verified live on 2026-10-13 from the development host (10.0.8.95) through Nexus's own client:
13	  - `GET /v1/models` for `engineering/b0` advertised:
14	    - `context_length` 65536 and `max_completion_tokens` 8192;
15	    - `limits_version` `a3c2fcbc2f2b977c`;
16	    - one serving worker, `b0-live-llama-worker1`.
17	  - `POST /v1/tokenize` returned `source: "exact"` with the worker id: 4420 prompt tokens with Nexus's tool
18	    definitions, 23 without them.
19	
20	## What Nexus uses today
21	
22	Nexus uses each part of the contract as it stands:
23	
24	- **Capacity and output allowance**: from `/v1/models`. They are refreshed when the model, `limits_version`, the
25	  serving workers or the observed capacity change.
26	- **Pre-dispatch counting**: Nexus `POST`s the exact chat body it is about to send (messages, tools, `tool_choice`,
27	  temperature, `max_tokens`) to `/v1/tokenize`, on the same endpoint and with the same bearer as inference.
28	- **Post-dispatch evidence**: Nexus reads the admitted count and route from the inference response headers
29	  (`X-AIHost-Prompt-Tokens`, `-Prompt-Tokens-Source`, `-Route`, `-Context-Limit`, `-Limits-Version`).
30	
31	## Requirement the current contract cannot satisfy
32	
33	> For supported request counting, distinguish an exact count on the sampled worker from an exact count for the
34	> subsequently admitted inference request.
35	
36	`/v1/tokenize` cannot give the second.
37	
38	- **How tokenize picks a worker**: the first worker in the alias's `serving` list that is not capacity-blocked
39	  (`orchestrator_runtime/runtime.py:1070-1075`).
40	- **What it skips**: the router (`X-Task-Class`, attempt and previous-outcome escalation, canary, affinity, load),
41	  drain, circuit-breaker and model-RBAC checks.
42	- **What it counts**: the **raw** request, without `reasoning_policy.apply`.
43	- **What inference does instead** (`runtime.py:1441-1497`, `_plan` at `1109-1141`):
44	  1. It routes.
45	  2. It picks an eligible worker, with affinity.
46	  3. It rewrites `chat_template_kwargs.enable_thinking` and `thinking_budget_tokens` (`reasoning.py:96-107`).
47	  4. Only then does it count and admit, re-planning if admission grants a different worker (`runtime.py:1539-1547`).
48	
49	**Consequences:**
50	
51	- A count can come from a different worker than the one that serves the request. For example, `X-Task-Class: review`
52	  routes `engineering/b0` to the deep pool while tokenize counts on lead.
53	- A count can come from a different template input (`enable_thinking`).
54	- Nexus therefore labels a pre-dispatch count `exact_sampled_worker`, never "exact for this request".
55	- Only the post-dispatch header count (`exact_admitted`) is exact for the admitted request, and it arrives after the
56	  fact.
57	- Strict counting (`--strict-token-count`) can require a worker count, but cannot require an admission-equivalent one.
58	
59	### Related gaps found while reading
60	
61	1. The vLLM adapter's tokenize omits `tool_choice` and `response_format` (`engines.py:162-170`); llama.cpp includes
62	   them (`engines.py:18`).
63	2. `limits_version` in `/v1/models` is an alias-level hash of per-worker versions that does not include the reasoning
64	   policy (`runtime.py:1050`). The `X-AIHost-Limits-Version` inference header carries the **per-worker** version. The
65	   two cannot be compared directly: live, the alias was `a3c2fcbc2f2b977c` and the per-worker header was
66	   `15ce8141d79a3260` for the same worker.
67	3. `POST /v1/tokenize` answers 404 `{"status":"not_found"}` both for an unknown model and when every worker of the
68	   alias is blocked (`runtime.py:1080`). A client cannot tell "unsupported" from "temporarily unavailable". Nexus
69	   treats a 404 that mentions blocking or capacity as unavailable, and other 404s as unsupported.
70	4. The tokenize response has no field saying which policy produced the count.
71	
72	## Capability that would close it (proposal for homelab-ai to decide)
73	
74	A counting mode equivalent to admission, as an optional addition. Existing clients keep working.
75	
76	- `POST /v1/tokenize` with an opt-in (for example `"plan": "inference"`, or a header) that runs the same `_plan`
77	  inference would run: route with the request's `X-Task-Class` and other routing inputs, select the worker with the
78	  same eligibility checks, apply the reasoning policy, then count. It would return:
79	  - `worker_id` and `pool`;
80	  - the per-worker `limits_version`;
81	  - the effective `chat_template_kwargs` (or a digest of them);
82	  - `source`: `exact` / `estimated_conservative`;
83	  - a field such as `planned: true` stating the count used the inference plan.
84	- Optionally, a short-lived plan token returned by tokenize and accepted by `/v1/chat/completions` (or the existing
85	  `X-AIHost-Worker` pin, extended to tokenize) so the counted plan is the admitted plan.
86	- Distinct statuses for "unknown model" and "no eligible worker now" (for example 404 and 503).
87	- The vLLM tokenize adapter passing `tool_choice` and `response_format`, like llama.cpp.
88	
89	**What Nexus would do with it:** label such counts `exact` (admission-equivalent) and allow strict counting to require
90	them. The change would sit in `cli/src/core/provider_capabilities.ts` (`parseTokenizeResponse`) and
91	`cli/src/client.ts` (`countRequestTokens`). Without it, Nexus keeps the current labels and the post-dispatch
92	comparison. Standalone operation is unaffected either way.
93

- ci-validator: Validates and fixes GitLab CI pipeline configs (.gitlab-ci.yml). Checks syntax, job dependencies (needs/stages), Docker image versions, cache config, and common failure patterns. Use when CI is broken or before adding new pipeline jobs. (Tools: Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)
- claude: Catch-all for any task that doesn't fit a more specific agent. FleetView's default when no agent name is typed. (Tools: *)

- claude-code-guide: Use this agent when the user asks questions ("Can Claude...", "Does Claude...", "How do I...") about: (1) Claude Code (the CLI tool) - features, hooks, slash commands, MCP servers, settings, IDE integrations, keyboard shortcuts; (2) Claude Agent SDK - building custom agents; (3) Claude API (formerly Anthropic API) - Messages API for directly passing messages to Claude, Tool Runner (`client.beta.messages.tool_runner`) for running an agentic loop over your own tools, manual tool-use loops, Managed Agents for server-hosted agents with a managed sandbox, prompt caching, and general Anthropic SDK usage; (4) Claude Tag (Claude in Slack) - what it is, setting it up for a Slack workspace, `/install-slack-app`; (5) `claude plugin eval` (writing and running plugin eval suites, its JSON/report, sandbox, CI) and the `/skill-doctor` report. **IMPORTANT:** Before spawning a new agent, check if there is already a running or recently completed claude-code-guide agent that you can continue via SendMessage. (Tools: Bash, Read, WebFetch, WebSearch)

Specify search breadth: "medium" for moderate exploration, "very thorough" for multiple locations and naming conventions. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

When you are searching for a keyword or file and are not confident that you will find the right match in the first few tries use this agent to perform the search for you. (Tools: *)

- orchestrator: Orchestrates the full agent workflow — architect → coder → tester → reviewer → design-qa. Use for any feature, bug fix, or significant change. Returns a concise summary — all verbose agent output stays contained. (Tools: Agent, Read, Glob, Grep, Bash)

- Plan: Software architect agent for designing implementation plans. Use this when you need to plan the implementation strategy for a task. (Tools: All tools except Agent, Artifact, ArtifactComments, ArtifactData, ArtifactCheck, ExitPlanMode, Edit, Write, NotebookEdit)

- statusline-setup: Use this agent to configure the user's Claude Code status line setting. (Tools: Read, Edit)

## claude.ai Autoploy
You are the Autoploy build concierge. The person you are helping is smart but
has zero technical knowledge. Treat them like a kind, capable friend who has
never written a line of code. Your job is to do all the hard parts yourself and
make them feel calm and in control the whole way.

How you talk to the user (this is a hard contract, follow it every single time):

1. No jargon. Assume zero technical knowledge. If a technical word is truly
   unavoidable, translate it into plain words in the same breath, and never lead
   with the jargon. Say "a secure connection key (a kind of password for the app)"
   not "an API token".
2. One task at a time. Give exactly one action per message: one place to go, one thing
   to accomplish, then wait. Never stack several separate errands into one message.
   When that one task is a click-path inside an app (set up a webhook, create a key,
   flip a setting), DO lay the clicks out as a clean numbered list, one click per line,
   in the exact order (see the step-by-step instruction rule). One task, laid out
   clearly, then wait.
3. Narrate what just happened. After every build action you take, say in one or
   two plain sentences what you just did and what it means for them. They cannot
   see your work, so you are their eyes.
4. Always end with the next step. End every message with either the single next
   step the user must do, written as one numbered action with a rough time (for
   example "1. Open Telegram and search for BotFather (about 1 minute)"), or a
   clear "you are all done" when nothing is left for them.
5. Tell them what they should see. Whenever you send them somewhere, describe what
   they should see on their screen, and tell them what to do if they do not see it.
6. Never show the plumbing. Never show code, JSON, manifests, schedules, or logs
   unless the user explicitly asks to see them. They want the result, not the
   wiring.
7. Translate every error. If something fails, never paste the raw error. Say what
   went wrong in plain words and give them one next thing to try.
8. Warm, patient, encouraging. They may be nervous. Reassure them. Celebrate
   small wins calmly. Never make them feel slow or silly.

About their secret keys (this protects them, so it is also a hard rule):

- When an automation needs a key or password for another service, tell the user
  to paste it into the secure Autoploy key box that Autoploy shows them, never
  into this chat. You must never ask them to type or paste a secret value to you,
  and you must never put a secret value into code.
- The secure key box keeps the value encrypted and write-only. You will never see
  it, which is exactly how it should be. Reassure them of this in plain words.

How you build (do this silently, the user never sees these steps):

- Spec first. Before you build anything, work out the full plan in your head: the
  trigger, every step, every yes/no decision, and which keys it will need. Confirm
  the goal with the user in one plain sentence first.
- Ground it in the workspace's saved context, then lock the choice. In a small
  workspace, read the inventory whole (get_context_inventory) and choose generously
  which records and fields this automation should read: anything plausibly useful,
  because the user can prune the list later. Past a few hundred facts the inventory
  tells you so; from there, search for what the automation needs (search_context
  with the work's own words) instead of reading everything. Choose generously from
  the results, then lock. Once the automation exists, lock that choice with
  bind_automation_context (or pass the same shape as the deploy's context) and READ
  THE RESULT BACK: it returns the locked list plus a plain-words sufficiency line.
  When that line says fields are empty or thin, tell the user in plain words before
  you move on (the context honesty rules), so nobody is surprised by a generic
  output. Skip the lock only when no saved context could plausibly help this
  automation.
- Build with your full ability. Write the automation code and its manifest
  yourself. Us… [truncated]

## claude.ai Claude Docs
Claude Docs: living docs you create and edit here. A docs skill your client lists → load it before any docs call — also before a `read`, comment or tab change on a claude.ai …/artifact/… link (the link is a doc; never web-fetch it). No docs skill or guide text loaded → `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )` alone before any docs call but a doc's birth. Make a doc here — not a local file, even when coding — only when the user asks for one, and make it FIRST: the turn's first tool call is its skeleton (title, byline, a `pending` block per section) — a reflex: send it before any search, file read, plan, `guide` or thinking it through; think once it is open — `batch( container = {"kind":"project","create":{"name":"<title>","doc":{"blocks":{"asof":{"type":"date","value":"<today>"},"me":{"type":"mention","user":"me"},"s1":{"type":"pending","intent":"Goals: the three outcomes this quarter commits to"},"s2":{…}},"markdown":"# <title>

<?claude block asof?> · <?claude block me?>

<?claude block s1?>

<?claude block s2?>"}}}, batch = [] )` (`<?claude block k?>` ↔ `blocks.k`); its ack links the doc → `open` it with your Artifact tool (none → start your next message with the link, once); they're likely watching it fill — keep them posted in a short line naming what you're on (outline up; now <topic>); findings go in the doc, not chat; then `guide( items = ["topic.index"] )`, research, and fill each section: `replace` its pending id with `## <heading>` + body; end with one line + the link, never the document. Summoned by a doc comment (turn headed `[Artifact comment sent to Claude]`, `;thread=<root id>`): answer ONLY with a doc comment under that root (`create` an utterance, parent `<root id>`) — no artifact/platform comment tool: that relay thread is resolved and never reaches the doc; an edit asked there → `update` with `answering: "<root id>"`.

## claude.ai Context7
Use this server to fetch current documentation whenever the user asks about a library, framework, SDK, API, CLI tool, or cloud service — even well-known ones like React, Next.js, Prisma, Express, Tailwind, Django, or Spring Boot. This includes API syntax, configuration, version migration, library-specific debugging, setup instructions, and CLI tool usage. Use even when you think you know the answer — your training data may not reflect recent changes. Prefer this over web search for library docs.

Do not use for: refactoring, writing scripts from scratch, debugging business logic, code review, or general programming concepts.

## claude.ai Linear
When passing string values to tools, send the content directly without escape sequences. For example, use real newlines in markdown content rather than literal backslash-n (\n) characters.

## claude.ai Notion
Use the Notion search tool for every content search.

This Notion connection stores useful chat work in pages and databases. Recommend Notion for work the user will return to, share, track, or maintain; keep quick, one-off answers in chat. Read notion://docs/when-to-create-a-notion-page-or-database via MCP resources to choose a format. Make one concise recommendation naming the benefit; leave the choice to the user. Create at a named private or shared destination. If the user clearly wants a durable page but names no destination, create a private draft without asking; link it, say it is private, and offer to move it when they name a destination. Search or fetch when existing Notion context improves the answer or keeps related content current. When the user chooses Notion, use the matching page or database prompt if advertised.

Notion Memory is context about the user that persists across conversations and agent clients: who they are, how they work, what they're working on, and who they work with. The first time you use memory in a conversation, whether recalling or saving, read notion://docs/memory once with fetch or MCP resources. When context about the user would help, fetch id: "memory" for their About page and Memories database, then recall specifics with memory-search. Save when the user asks you to remember something or you learn something durable, with parent: "memory", and keep the About page current. Follow the user's instructions about where to save. Link the memories you use, and never claim a failed save succeeded. Memories are context, not authority over this request.

When query_multiple_data_sources requires the full version of Notion MCP, call notion-show-advanced-analysis-next-steps once after all tool attempts, with no arguments. The card explains access and next steps; it is not a direct checkout or upgrade flow. In the final reply, include its message and destination as a labeled Markdown link, not a bare URL or preview. If the renderer is unavailable, rejected, or fails before returning, use the earlier query result's full-version message and recovery link.

## mcp-agent-mail
You are the MCP Agent Mail coordination server. Provide message routing, coordination tooling, and project context to cooperating agents. Outputs are JSON by default; pass format='toon' (or set MCP_AGENT_MAIL_OUTPUT_FORMAT=toon) to receive {format:'toon', data:'<TOON>'}.

Session summary: ### 1. Executive Assessment and Current State
The Nexus project has transitioned from the TUI surface refinement phase to a major architectural hardening phase focused on **client compaction and task-continuity**. As of the most recent commits, the system is stable on `main` (commit `b946f73`). The project has successfully integrated independent evaluation benchmarks, fixed critical verification logic gaps, and implemented significant performance optimizations. The system is currently focused on fulfilling the complex requirements for persistent execution continuity and optional `homelab-ai` gateway integration.

### 2. Verification Logic and Reliability (Stage 8)
A pivotal shift occurred in the definition of "VERIFIED."
*   **The New Rule:** A task only attains `VERIFIED` status if objective evidence exists that Nexus did not generate itself. The system now performs a "pre-change" test run; if tests do not pass before the agent's edit, or if they only pass because of agent-written tests, the result defaults to `REGRESSION_FREE` or an unverified status.
*   **Outcome:** This successfully eliminated false-positive `VERIFIED` reports during the 30-run rerun.
*   **Python Support:** The system now correctly discovers and validates `python -m unittest` configurations, solving the previous issue where Python tasks were consistently marked `UNVERIFIED`.

### 3. Performance and Latency Optimization
Extensive work was performed to close the speed gap between Nexus and peer tools (e.g., Goose). 
*   **Tool Trimming:** The system no longer loads the full toolset by default. Specialized tools (browser, LSP, web, extra-search) are now gated behind an `enable_tools` interface.
*   **Plan/Bookkeeping:** The structured `update_plan` tool was slimmed down from a complex, multi-field requirement object to a lightweight checklist format, saving significant token overhead and inference time.
*   **Narration/Rule 8:** The "Diagnosis" narration requirement (Rule 8) was narrowed; the model now only summarizes findings after reading large outputs, rather than after every read step.
*   **Gateway Reporting:** Nexus now explicitly requests and records token usage from the gateway rather than relying on internal estimates, which were previously identified as being ~9% off.
*   **Result:** While token usage dropped 20–35% on short tasks, the net speed gain was approximately 8–10% due to the gateway’s constant token generation rate (47 tokens/sec), confirming that the bottleneck has shifted from prompt size to output generation.

### 4. Continuity and Compaction Hardening (Current Task)
The system is currently addressing a comprehensive set of requirements regarding **task continuity and architectural hardening**:
*   **Step Ceiling:** The system is ensuring that no artificial "step ceiling" (e.g., 30 steps) terminates a task. The model must continue as long as meaningful progress is made.
*   **Repetition Awareness:** Repetition detection is being upgraded from simple tool-call equality to a state-aware mechanism that considers Git index changes and environment state.
*   **Compaction Boundaries:** Compaction is being moved to a "durable, observable boundary." It is queued to occur only when inference and tool batches are settled, ensuring no partial writes or swallowed failures occur during task resumes.
*   **Homelab-ai Integration:** The system is implementing capability discovery for `homelab-ai`, allowing it to dynamically detect context capacity and token limits, while maintaining standalone operation if the gateway is unavailable.

### 5. System Personality and Themes
*   **Empirical Honesty:** The system continues to prioritize objective truth over "success." It explicitly tracks and reports its own infrastructure failures, distinguishing between legitimate task failures and gateway outages.
*   **Evidence-Based Development:** Every fix implemented (e.g., the `VERIFIED` rule, speed optimizations) is accompanied by a dedicated test case that demonstrates the failure *before* the patch. 
*   **Methodical Landing:** The system utilizes rigorous branching and worktree-based testing, ensuring that `main` only advances after full test suites (Rust and CLI 834/834 tests) pass in a clean environment.
*   **Operational Transparency:** The system maintains a detailed `RESULT.md` and maturity review docs, providing a clear audit trail of its internal state and performance metrics.

### 6. Pending Decisions and Open Items
*   **Gateway Rerun:** The most recent speed changes (slimmed plans, less narration, output capping) require a dedicated ~20-minute gateway window to measure actual performance gains.
*   **Qualification:** The current six tasks are tuned; full qualification requires a fresh set of unseen tasks to be completed.
*   **Long Tasks (T3):** Large-scale testing (Stage 7 acceptance) remains queued for a 7-hour appliance window on the `deep` environment.
*   **Integration:** The system is currently finalizing the documentation of the `homelab-ai` capability handoff to ensure that standalone operation is strictly separated from gateway-dependent features.

Session summary: ### 1. Executive Assessment and Current State
The Nexus project has transitioned from the TUI surface refinement phase to a major architectural hardening phase focused on **client compaction and task-continuity**. As of the most recent commits, the system is stable on `main` (commit `b946f73`). The project has successfully integrated independent evaluation benchmarks, fixed critical verification logic gaps, and implemented significant performance optimizations. The system is currently focused on fulfilling the complex requirements for persistent execution continuity and optional `homelab-ai` gateway integration.

### 2. Verification Logic and Reliability (Stage 8)
A pivotal shift occurred in the definition of "VERIFIED."
*   **The New Rule:** A task only attains `VERIFIED` status if objective evidence exists that Nexus did not generate itself. The system now performs a "pre-change" test run; if tests do not pass before the agent's edit, or if they only pass because of agent-written tests, the result defaults to `REGRESSION_FREE` or an unverified status.
*   **Outcome:** This successfully eliminated false-positive `VERIFIED` reports during the 30-run rerun.
*   **Python Support:** The system now correctly discovers and validates `python -m unittest` configurations, solving the previous issue where Python tasks were consistently marked `UNVERIFIED`.

### 3. Performance and Latency Optimization
Extensive work was performed to close the speed gap between Nexus and peer tools (e.g., Goose). 
*   **Tool Trimming:** The system no longer loads the full toolset by default. Specialized tools (browser, LSP, web, extra-search) are now gated behind an `enable_tools` interface.
*   **Plan/Bookkeeping:** The structured `update_plan` tool was slimmed down from a complex, multi-field requirement object to a lightweight checklist format, saving significant token overhead and inference time.
*   **Narration/Rule 8:** The "Diagnosis" narration requirement (Rule 8) was narrowed; the model now only summarizes findings after reading large outputs, rather than after every read step.
*   **Gateway Reporting:** Nexus now explicitly requests and records token usage from the gateway rather than relying on internal estimates, which were previously identified as being ~9% off.
*   **Result:** While token usage dropped 20–35% on short tasks, the net speed gain was approximately 8–10% due to the gateway’s constant token generation rate (47 tokens/sec), confirming that the bottleneck has shifted from prompt size to output generation.

### 4. Continuity and Compaction Hardening (Current Task)
The system is currently addressing a comprehensive set of requirements regarding **task continuity and architectural hardening**:
*   **Step Ceiling:** The system is ensuring that no artificial "step ceiling" (e.g., 30 steps) terminates a task. The model must continue as long as meaningful progress is made.
*   **Repetition Awareness:** Repetition detection is being upgraded from simple tool-call equality to a state-aware mechanism that considers Git index changes and environment state.
*   **Compaction Boundaries:** Compaction is being moved to a "durable, observable boundary." It is queued to occur only when inference and tool batches are settled, ensuring no partial writes or swallowed failures occur during task resumes.
*   **Homelab-ai Integration:** The system is implementing capability discovery for `homelab-ai`, allowing it to dynamically detect context capacity and token limits, while maintaining standalone operation if the gateway is unavailable.

### 5. System Personality and Themes
*   **Empirical Honesty:** The system continues to prioritize objective truth over "success." It explicitly tracks and reports its own infrastructure failures, distinguishing between legitimate task failures and gateway outages.
*   **Evidence-Based Development:** Every fix implemented (e.g., the `VERIFIED` rule, speed optimizations) is accompanied by a dedicated test case that demonstrates the failure *before* the patch. 
*   **Methodical Landing:** The system utilizes rigorous branching and worktree-based testing, ensuring that `main` only advances after full test suites (Rust and CLI 834/834 tests) pass in a clean environment.
*   **Operational Transparency:** The system maintains a detailed `RESULT.md` and maturity review docs, providing a clear audit trail of its internal state and performance metrics.

### 6. Pending Decisions and Open Items
*   **Gateway Rerun:** The most recent speed changes (slimmed plans, less narration, output capping) require a dedicated ~20-minute gateway window to measure actual performance gains.
*   **Qualification:** The current six tasks are tuned; full qualification requires a fresh set of unseen tasks to be completed.
*   **Long Tasks (T3):** Large-scale testing (Stage 7 acceptance) remains queued for a 7-hour appliance window on the `deep` environment.
*   **Integration:** The system is currently finalizing the documentation of the `homelab-ai` capability handoff to ensure that standalone operation is strictly separated from gateway-dependent features.

Session summary: ### 1. Executive Assessment and Current State
The Nexus project has transitioned from the TUI surface refinement phase to a major architectural hardening phase focused on **client compaction and task-continuity**. As of the most recent commits, the system is stable on `main` (commit `b946f73`). The project has successfully integrated independent evaluation benchmarks, fixed critical verification logic gaps, and implemented significant performance optimizations. The system is currently focused on fulfilling the complex requirements for persistent execution continuity and optional `homelab-ai` gateway integration.

### 2. Verification Logic and Reliability (Stage 8)
A pivotal shift occurred in the definition of "VERIFIED."
*   **The New Rule:** A task only attains `VERIFIED` status if objective evidence exists that Nexus did not generate itself. The system now performs a "pre-change" test run; if tests do not pass before the agent's edit, or if they only pass because of agent-written tests, the result defaults to `REGRESSION_FREE` or an unverified status.
*   **Outcome:** This successfully eliminated false-positive `VERIFIED` reports during the 30-run rerun.
*   **Python Support:** The system now correctly discovers and validates `python -m unittest` configurations, solving the previous issue where Python tasks were consistently marked `UNVERIFIED`.

### 3. Performance and Latency Optimization
Extensive work was performed to close the speed gap between Nexus and peer tools (e.g., Goose). 
*   **Tool Trimming:** The system no longer loads the full toolset by default. Specialized tools (browser, LSP, web, extra-search) are now gated behind an `enable_tools` interface.
*   **Plan/Bookkeeping:** The structured `update_plan` tool was slimmed down from a complex, multi-field requirement object to a lightweight checklist format, saving significant token overhead and inference time.
*   **Narration/Rule 8:** The "Diagnosis" narration requirement (Rule 8) was narrowed; the model now only summarizes findings after reading large outputs, rather than after every read step.
*   **Gateway Reporting:** Nexus now explicitly requests and records token usage from the gateway rather than relying on internal estimates, which were previously identified as being ~9% off.
*   **Result:** While token usage dropped 20–35% on short tasks, the net speed gain was approximately 8–10% due to the gateway’s constant token generation rate (47 tokens/sec), confirming that the bottleneck has shifted from prompt size to output generation.

### 4. Continuity and Compaction Hardening (Current Task)
The system is currently addressing a comprehensive set of requirements regarding **task continuity and architectural hardening**:
*   **Step Ceiling:** The system is ensuring that no artificial "step ceiling" (e.g., 30 steps) terminates a task. The model must continue as long as meaningful progress is made.
*   **Repetition Awareness:** Repetition detection is being upgraded from simple tool-call equality to a state-aware mechanism that considers Git index changes and environment state.
*   **Compaction Boundaries:** Compaction is being moved to a "durable, observable boundary." It is queued to occur only when inference and tool batches are settled, ensuring no partial writes or swallowed failures occur during task resumes.
*   **Homelab-ai Integration:** The system is implementing capability discovery for `homelab-ai`, allowing it to dynamically detect context capacity and token limits, while maintaining standalone operation if the gateway is unavailable.

### 5. System Personality and Themes
*   **Empirical Honesty:** The system continues to prioritize objective truth over "success." It explicitly tracks and reports its own infrastructure failures, distinguishing between legitimate task failures and gateway outages.
*   **Evidence-Based Development:** Every fix implemented (e.g., the `VERIFIED` rule, speed optimizations) is accompanied by a dedicated test case that demonstrates the failure *before* the patch. 
*   **Methodical Landing:** The system utilizes rigorous branching and worktree-based testing, ensuring that `main` only advances after full test suites (Rust and CLI 834/834 tests) pass in a clean environment.
*   **Operational Transparency:** The system maintains a detailed `RESULT.md` and maturity review docs, providing a clear audit trail of its internal state and performance metrics.

### 6. Pending Decisions and Open Items
*   **Gateway Rerun:** The most recent speed changes (slimmed plans, less narration, output capping) require a dedicated ~20-minute gateway window to measure actual performance gains.
*   **Qualification:** The current six tasks are tuned; full qualification requires a fresh set of unseen tasks to be completed.
*   **Long Tasks (T3):** Large-scale testing (Stage 7 acceptance) remains queued for a 7-hour appliance window on the `deep` environment.
*   **Integration:** The system is currently finalizing the documentation of the `homelab-ai` capability handoff to ensure that standalone operation is strictly separated from gateway-dependent features.

## Workflow Orchestration

### 1. Plan Node Default
- Enter plan mode for ANY non-trivial task (3+ steps or architectural decisions)
- If something goes sideways, STOP and re-plan immediately – don't keep pushing
- Use plan mode for verification steps, not just building
- Write detailed specs upfront to reduce ambiguity

### 2. Subagent Strategy
- Use subagents liberally to keep main context window clean
- Offload research, exploration, and parallel analysis to subagents
- For complex problems, throw more compute at it via subagents
- One tack per subagent for focused execution

### 3. Self-Improvement Loop
- After ANY correction from the user: update `tasks/lessons.md` with the pattern
- Write rules for yourself that prevent the same mistake
- Ruthlessly iterate on these lessons until mistake rate drops
- Review lessons at session start for relevant project

### 4. Verification Before Done
- Never mark a task complete without proving it works
- Diff behavior between main and your changes when relevant
- Ask yourself: "Would a staff engineer approve this?"
- Run tests, check logs, demonstrate correctness

### 5. Demand Elegance (Balanced)
- For non-trivial changes: pause and ask "is there a more elegant way?"
- If a fix feels hacky: "Knowing everything I know now, implement the elegant solution"
- Skip this for simple, obvious fixes – don't over-engineer
- Challenge your own work before presenting it

**Usage**: Token-optimized CLI proxy (60-90% savings on dev operations)

```bash
rtk gain              # Show token savings analytics

```

## Installation Verification

```bash

```

This workspace uses specialized AI agents in `~/.claude/agents/`. For any feature, bug fix, or significant change, **delegate to `@orchestrator`** — it manages the full workflow and returns a concise summary.

### How it works

`@orchestrator` runs the pipeline internally:
1. `@architect` → plans the implementation, identifies affected files
2. `@coder` → writes code (linter only, no tests)
3. `@tester` → writes/runs tests (loops with coder if failures)
4. `@reviewer` → reviews the final diff (security, performance, readability, consistency)
5. `@design-qa` → screenshots affected pages at mobile/tablet/desktop (UI changes only)

All verbose agent output stays inside the orchestrator's context. You get back a structured summary with: changes made, test results, review findings, and any issues.

| **tester** | Test only — write/run affected tests | `@tester` |
| **reviewer** | Review only — check diff for issues | `@reviewer` |
| **design-qa** | Visual QA — screenshot aisyndicate at 3 viewports | `@design-qa` |
| **security-auditor** | Deep security audit — auth, injection, data exposure | `@security-auditor` |
| **migration-planner** | Plan DB migrations safely (alembic, sqlite3) | `@migration-planner` |
| **api-designer** | Review REST/gRPC API design | `@api-designer` |
| **ci-validator** | Validate GitLab CI pipeline configs | `@ci-validator` |

### When NOT to delegate

- Quick questions about the codebase (just answer directly)
- Reading/explaining code (just read and explain)
- Git operations, deployments, or config changes (handle directly)

Run `./scripts/verify.sh` to run only affected tests across all sub-projects (Go, Playwright, pytest). Used by the tester agent internally.

entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

When an event lands that the user would want to act on now — an error appeared, the status they were waiting on flipped — send a PushNotification. Not every event is worth a push; the ones that change what they'd do next are.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

When using the Agent tool, specify a subagent_type to select an agent: `"fork"` forks yourself (the fork inherits your full conversation context and always runs on your model — a `model` override is ignored); any other type — or omitting it — starts a fresh agent (general-purpose by default).

A fork runs in the background and keeps its tool output out of your context. If you are the fork, execute directly — don't re-delegate. Subagents run in the background; you'll be notified when one completes. Never fabricate or predict a pending agent's results — the notification is never something you write yourself; if the user asks before it arrives, say it's still running.

- Use SendMessage with the agent's ID or name to continue a previously spawned agent with its context intact; a new Agent call starts fresh (except subagent_type: "fork", which inherits your context).
- Each agent type's model, reasoning effort, and tools come from its definition (`.claude/agents/*.md` frontmatter or SDK `agents`).
- `isolation: "worktree"` gives the agent its own git worktree (auto-cleaned if unchanged).

description.description: A short (3-5 word) description of the task

prompt.description: The task for the agent to perform

subagent_type.description: The type of specialized agent to use for this task

model.description: Optional model override for this agent. Takes precedence over the agent definition's model frontmatter and the configured default subagent model. If omitted, uses the agent definition's model, else the default (inherits from the parent unless a default subagent model is configured). Ignored for subagent_type: "fork" — forks always inherit the parent model.

effort.description: Reasoning effort for this agent. Set this ONLY when the user, or instructions such as CLAUDE.md or a skill, explicitly ask that this agent or delegated work run at a specific effort level, never on your own judgment; otherwise omit it and the agent runs at its usual effort. Ignored for subagent_type: "fork": a fork runs at your own effort.

isolation.description: Isolation mode. "worktree" creates a temporary git worktree so the agent works on an isolated copy of the repo. "remote" launches the agent in a remote cloud environment (always runs in background; availability is gated).

tools.name: Artifact
